item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded: It should actually be fairly easy to determine if the cookies are causing the future or just predicting it, using statistical inference. It's caused/predicted enough deaths to determine if the rate of death among users is out of line with expectation. If it is, there's a good chance the cookies are at fault. If it's not, then at worst it's changing the "how" but not the "when".

item.title: Re:
item.content:encoded:
The third test is easy: put a D-class in a room, have him open the cookie and hold out the message blindfolded, remove the message without anyone seeing it, kill the D-class, then read it. (It won't predict things which happen after their death, presumably.)

The first test is trickier, but not impossible. Here's a rough example, though it needs work: Put a D-class in a situation where he has to guess which number a researcher is thinking - either 1 or 2 - or he dies. Inform him completely of this, then have him open a cookie. The researcher will read the message after the D-class reads it: if it details which number is "correct", then the researcher will think of the other number instead. (A control experiment could be done where the researcher does not see the cookie's predictions.) If an improbable event happens which forces the researcher to choose a number that the cookie predicts, then this SCP is likely capable of probability manipulation.

Damn, I need to think this through a bit more.

item.title: Re:
item.content:encoded:
That's not a bad idea.

We can give a cookie to a Class D, place him in a Schrödinger's Cat situation with two very different outcomes (say, death by SCP-230 or SCP-682), and extract the fortune from the containment area without breaking the quantum superposition. Then we could see what the formula reads, a measure of how omnipotent this SCP really is.

Or maybe I'm overthinking things.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
It seems a little too benevolent, though fortune cookies are designed that way, anyway. Seconded on cross-testing with humanoid SCPs, but there should also be some limited testing on the following inquiries:

  • Since the fortunes often indicate notable and close events, do the fortunes actually cause them?
  • Do the fortunes come true if the opener does not read them?
  • Do the fortunes come true if nobody reads them?
  • Does SCP-377 exhibit sentience?

I'd be willing to construct a battery of tests, though I've never done something like this before.
